Tip1: Right-click a column header to sort its tickets. By title, priority, assignee or date. The choice is shared with the project board.
Tip2: Drag a ticket onto another one to turn it into a sub-ticket. The 📂 badge on the parent opens its own sub-kanban.
Tip3: Ctrl+Z undoes your last board actions. Moves, deletes, renames, priority changes. Up to 30 steps back.
Tip4: The search understands tokens. Try #42, @assignee, priority:critical, label:bug or by:owner.
Tip5: Schedule a ticket with ⏰. It will move to its target column by itself when the time comes.
Tip6: The home has two views, each with its own URL. The unified kanban lives at / and the project cards at /projects. Bookmark the one you prefer.
Tip7: Automations can call external services. The httpRequest action fills {ticketId}, {ticketTitle} or {now} for you.
Tip8: Chat with a ticket's assigned agent from its panel. The 💬 button keeps the ticket as context.
Tip9: KittyClaw has no authentication. Its agents run code on this machine. Keep it on localhost, with no tunnel or reverse proxy.
Tip10: Pause a project with ⏸ to stop its automations. Paused projects sink to the bottom of the home, collapsed.
Tip11: Paste an image straight into a description or a comment. It is uploaded and linked automatically.
Tip12: Write #42 in a comment to link a ticket. With #project-slug:7 the reference crosses projects.
Tip13: Everything the UI does is scriptable. The REST API is documented live at /api/docs.
Tip14: Esc closes overlays one at a time. Menu first, then editor, then panel. No mouse needed.
Tip15: Right-click a column, then choose Configure. Its role, color, user guidance, processor, actions, scheduled tasks and routing are all managed in one place.
Tip16: A project can contain several independent pipelines. Rename them safely: KittyClaw keeps stable identifiers for tickets and routing.
Tip17: A column processor claims one eligible ticket at a time. It runs its actions, optionally calls its agent, then routes the ticket from the result.
Tip18: Routing also protects manual moves. When a column declares destinations, the menu and drag-and-drop prevent skipping to an unexpected stage.
Tip19: Use the Owner action required role for a human decision. The ticket is highlighted, assigned to the Owner and shows the guidance needed to unblock it.
Tip20: Recurring work lives in a column's Scheduled tasks tab. The visual editor builds the frequency without asking you to write a cron expression.
Tip21: Project skills describe reusable technical and operational procedures. A processor can make them available, recommended or required for its generic agent.
Tip22: Each processor and scheduled task can choose its model. New instructions reuse your last choice, while an existing conversation always keeps its original model.
Tip23: A pipeline's orange badge counts its visible unread tickets. Right-click a column and choose Mark all as read to reset its count.
Tip24: A legacy automation board can be migrated with the wizard. Review its pipelines and columns step by step before launching the migration.
Tip25: The Costs page uses a cached report. Start with a quick date range, then filter by project, pipeline or model.
Tip26: On Costs, green means measured, striped orange means estimated, and the cyan-to-green gradient shows RTK savings.
Tip27: Enable RTK in project settings to condense command output before it reaches the agent. Estimated savings then appear on Costs.
Tip28: A runtime approval pauses the agent before a sensitive action. Open Approvals from the board to allow once, allow for the ticket or deny it.
Tip29: Enable worktrees in project settings to isolate each implementation. The ticket panel shows its branch, folder and integration status.
Tip30: Connect tickets with Blocked by and Blocks. Processors wait for dependencies to resolve before starting dependent work.
Tip31: In an Owner action required stage, the decision brief gathers the useful context. Accept, request a correction or stop without rereading the full history.
Tip32: Dashboard tiles can render Markdown, KPIs, charts, tables, timelines or Mermaid diagrams. Each tile has its own refresh interval.
